title: Rav Natan bar Abba (I)
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Hyman describes him as a student of Rav, citing his explanation of a teaching before Rav in Bava Metzia 41a and his reports in Beitzah 32b.
“Rav Natan bar Abba said in the name of Rav.” Three occurrences [ג״פ].

At the end of Jerusalem Talmud Avodah Zarah, chapter 2, Natan bar Ba tells Shmuel: “I know how to distinguish the roe of non-kosher fish from that of kosher fish: the former is round, the latter elongated.” Shmuel shows him a salpita; Natan calls it non-kosher. Shmuel says: “Calling a kosher one non-kosher does not trouble me, but you will end by calling a non-kosher one kosher.” Hyman reports that Tosafot, under “Amar Rava” on Avodah Zarah 40a, cites this passage under the name Rav Natan bar Rava. Hyman identifies him as the same person, saying that Rava and Abba are one name.

notes.text: The terse ג״פ is read as “three occurrences”; precisely which three occurrences Hyman counts is not established. The fish-roe warning is Shmuel’s response to Natan. The Abba/Rava equation is Hyman’s identification.

No new primary scalar was returned or concordance performed. ג״פ contextually means three occurrences, but which three is unresolved. The dialogue has Shmuel showing the salpita, Natan calling it non-kosher, and Shmuel warning that calling a kosher one non-kosher does not trouble ME, but he will end by calling a non-kosher one kosher. Salpita remains unidentified. Hyman’s disciple claim and Abba/Rava personal equation are attributed, not new chronology or identity findings. Natan bar Ba and untitled Shmuel remain distinct source forms; all explicit full Rav titles remain. The supplied כב״ם is retained in the source beside the contextual Bava Metzia41a expansion; Tosafot’s Amar Rava40a and the unspecified count are inherited and unverified here.

The consulted Beitzah 32b has three teachings with this formula, on a Festival wick, wealthy Babylonians, and relying on another’s table. These are the likely referents of the count beside the citation in Hyman’s print (III, p. 954). The consulted Bava Metzia 41a calls him Rabbi Natan bar Abba, whereas Hyman prints Rav. Jerusalem Talmud Avodah Zarah 2:9 includes Shmuel’s question about the salpita before Natan calls it non-kosher. Guggenheimer glosses the fish as salpe and translates Shmuel’s opening as a stronger expression of displeasure. The consulted Tosafot quotes Natan bar Rava without the title and explains the example as roe from a kosher fish. Hyman’s equation of the names remains his interpretation.
